title: Worksheet — Number Systems (Class 10 NIOS Mathematics)
instructions: Attempt all 10 questions in your notebook. Show every step of your work for the subjective questions; choose the single best option for MCQs. Answers without working will not receive full marks. Total time: 45 minutes.

questions.question: Which of the following is the smallest whole number?
questions.explanation: Whole numbers W = {0, 1, 2, ...}; the smallest is 0.

questions.question: Every integer is a rational number.
questions.explanation: Any integer n equals n/1, which is rational.

questions.question: The reciprocal of −5/8 is ____.
questions.explanation: Reciprocal of a/b is b/a, preserving sign: reciprocal of −5/8 is −8/5.

questions.question: Express −24/36 in standard (lowest) form:
questions.explanation: HCF(24, 36) = 12; divide both by 12 → −2/3 with positive denominator.

questions.question: Evaluate: (−2/3) + (5/6) − (1/2). Show all steps.
questions.explanation: Use a common denominator (LCM 6), then combine numerators and reduce.

questions.question: Find three rational numbers between 1/4 and 1/3.
questions.answer: Bring to a common denominator with extra room: 1/4 = 9/36, 1/3 = 12/36. Three rationals strictly between are 10/36 = 5/18, 11/36 and (using 144 as denominator) 41/144 = also between. So 5/18, 11/36 and 41/144 are three rationals strictly between 1/4 and 1/3. (Other valid answers exist; the key is to refine the denominator until at least three integers lie strictly between the rewritten numerators.)
questions.explanation: Rationals are dense — choose any common denominator d for which d × (1/3) − d × (1/4) ≥ 4 to leave at least three integer numerators between them.

questions.question: Without performing long division, decide whether 13/40 and 7/15 have terminating decimal expansions. Justify each decision.
questions.answer: 13/40: 40 = 2³ × 5. Lowest-terms denominator has only the primes 2 and 5, so the decimal terminates. (Indeed 13/40 = 0.325.) 7/15: 15 = 3 × 5. The factor 3 is not 2 or 5, so the decimal is non-terminating recurring. (Indeed 7/15 = 0.466... = 0.46̄.)
questions.explanation: Apply the rule: p/q (lowest terms) terminates iff q = 2^m × 5^n.

questions.question: Express 0.6̄ and 0.2̄7̄ (bar over the digits shown) as fractions in lowest terms. Show the algebraic manipulation in each case.
questions.answer: Part 1 — 0.6̄: Let x = 0.666... Multiply by 10: 10x = 6.666... Subtract: 10x − x = 6 → 9x = 6 → x = 6/9. Reduce by HCF 3: x = 2/3. So 0.6̄ = 2/3. Part 2 — 0.2̄7̄ (bar over 27): Let x = 0.272727... Multiply by 100 (because 2 digits repeat): 100x = 27.2727... Subtract: 100x − x = 27 → 99x = 27 → x = 27/99. Reduce by HCF 9: x = 3/11. So 0.2̄7̄ = 3/11.
questions.explanation: For an n-digit repeating block, multiply by 10^n then subtract the original to eliminate the recurring tail.

questions.question: (a) Verify the distributive property of multiplication over addition for rational numbers using a = 3/4, b = 1/3, c = 5/6. (b) Then state and verify which of the four 'addition' properties (closure, commutative, associative, additive identity) hold for rational numbers, giving a one-line example for each.
questions.answer: (a) Distributive: a(b + c) = ab + ac. LHS: (3/4) × (1/3 + 5/6) = (3/4) × (2/6 + 5/6) = (3/4) × (7/6) = 21/24 = 7/8. RHS: (3/4)(1/3) + (3/4)(5/6) = 3/12 + 15/24 = 6/24 + 15/24 = 21/24 = 7/8. LHS = RHS, so the property holds. (b) Closure: For any p/q, r/s ∈ Q, p/q + r/s ∈ Q. Example: 2/5 + 3/7 = 14/35 + 15/35 = 29/35 ∈ Q. Commutative: a + b = b + a. Example: 1/2 + 1/3 = 5/6 = 1/3 + 1/2. Associative: (a + b) + c = a + (b + c). Example with a = 1/2, b = 1/3, c = 1/4: (1/2 + 1/3) + 1/4 = 5/6 + 1/4 = 13/12; 1/2 + (1/3 + 1/4) = 1/2 + 7/12 = 13/12. Equal. Additive identity: there exists 0 ∈ Q with a + 0 = a. Example: 7/9 + 0 = 7/9. All four properties hold.
questions.explanation: Verifying a property algebraically with one numeric example is enough at this level.
